title: Cross-Validation
description: Estimate model performance with different cross-validation approaches
content:
**Cross-validation** is a technique used to evaluate a model by partitioning the dataset into subsets. Instead of relying on a single train-test split, the model is trained and validated multiple times on different partitions of the data, which makes the estimate of its performance more reliable.

> Common cross-validation schemes:
> • K-fold cross-validation
> • Leave-p-out cross-validation
> • Leave-one-out cross-validation
> • Chain cross-validation
> • Sliding window validation

With **k-fold cross-validation**, the dataset is separated into K folds. The model is trained on K − 1 folds and validated on the remaining one. This process is repeated K times, so each fold serves as a validation dataset exactly once.

With **leave-p-out cross-validation**, in each iteration, p samples are held out as the validation set, while the model is trained on the rest of the data. Its special case is **leave-one-out cross-validation**, where each fold is the size of one, so the model is validated on every single sample separately.

> Computational cost matters here: as the number of folds increases, the computational load increases linearly - there are as many training iterations as there are folds. That is why K-fold cross-validation is faster than leave-p-out cross-validation, which requires far more training iterations.

An effective approach to apply cross-validation in the realm of sequentially linked data (e.g., time series) is **chain cross-validation**: the model is iteratively trained on a subset of data and validated on the next data record, while the training subset keeps increasing. This respects the order of observations - the model is always validated on data that comes after its training data.

A variation of chain cross-validation is the **sliding window cross-validation** approach: after each iteration, the train and test window is moved forward by a fixed number of time steps, so the model always trains on a window of a fixed length.
